title: A sober K-hole
excerpt: A NSFW Edinburgh Fringe experience at McEwan Hall
body:
My friends and I pined and longed to see Reuben Kaye’s Kaye Hole for the last three years of the Fringe, but it was always programmed too late at night for us to make the last train home. We settled—although not really—for his cabaret shows instead and always said “next year”, “next year” for Kaye Hole. Well, we finally did it; we arranged accommodation in Edinburgh (thank you Sam and Emily) and took ourselves to this utterly debauched variety show. Let’s say it lived up to our expectations and then some. It may become the event that we aim to see every year from now on. Absolute carnage and queer joy.

Having studied in Edinburgh, I spent a lot of time in the buildings that host numerous Fringe shows in August. It’s always surreal to see the full staging of the next West End musical inside the basketball hall where I did gymnastics. Or the George Square lecture theatre, where I once copied maths equations from the chalkboard, hosting the audacious Police Cops. And while I wasn’t allowed to graduate at McEwan Hall (they dared to renovate it our year, gasp, and stuck us in Usher Hall instead), I was still fortunate enough to take exams there. I remember sitting nervously at my single island desk, trying not to be distracted by the stained glass, opulent murals, and intricate woodwork of this Italian Renaissance-style building while the paper loomed before me.

Each August, this grand auditorium sheds its usual purpose. Built for the solemn celebratory atmosphere of virtuous Edinburgh University graduates, it instead hosts some of the Fringe's biggest names. The flat floor is filled with temporary tiered seating leading right back to the front of the pew-style balcony mezzanine. The vibrant murals and biblical wisdom texts on the ceiling are covered with heavy black drapes, as if shielding them from the depravity to come. Even the original wood floor is boarded over for the night.

The Kaye Hole started rather gently: Trigger Happy, a plus-size Shrek burlesque character from Swamplesque, peeling off his layers and twirling nipple tassels off his plump bum cheeks. "Gently" is a relative word, of course. Everything is relative at Kaye Hole.

Rosie Jones was up next. When her microphone cut out, Reuben ran on to swap it for his working one, quickly unsheathed from its ponytail, and once she could actually be heard, she didn't miss a beat: "Even my microphone is disabled." Reuben, still standing at the side of the stage, doubled over laughing. Speaking of our conférencier, his bits between the acts were even looser and filthier than his “pre-watershed” cabaret show. Dressed in a sexy red bin bag and full glam, he cracked jokes, seductively sang a ballad on (yes, on) an audience member, and called out Assembly’s 60/40 financial split. A quadruple threat.

Birds followed; we had recently seen their performance at the Box, so we knew the setup: two women in bikinis and kaftans, chatting and sunbathing, ignoring the chaos building around them. But the original premise didn’t survive long. Water pistols came out, sunburnt skin peeled off in strips and tossed into the audience, and Reuben Kaye joined them on stage, clad in a pair of breasts spurting water for them to drink from. Chaos, entirely on schedule.

After another brief interlude from Reuben, we had the stunningly toned, scantily clad male acrobat/burlesque performer, Teva. Seducing the crowd with his raw strength and toned body suspended on straps hanging from the ceiling. It felt wholesome by comparison.

We’re about halfway through now, and this is where it tipped. A spinning-on-her-willy (ask me how) drag queen, a fire breather, and a clown in nothing but a loose vest appeared in the audience. Hoops were tossed out to us. Reuben distracted the room long enough for the clown to flip herself upside down on the corner of a safety railing. Legs akimbo, nude, with a pole rising from her nethers, a target for the audience to play hoop toss. The winners got shots of vodka served straight from Kaye’s mouth - consensually, mercifully.

Then a shift to something spellbindingly beautiful. A shaving lip-sync performance from Cirque du Soleil acrobat and ex-professional ballet dancer, David Pereira. He dropped his towel, covered every inch of skin in foam, and then held an impressively extended side split while running a razor from root to foot. Taint to toes. I don’t know how to describe it fully, but it was captivating. Something about his stage presence, impressive strength and flexibility, and the ludicrousness of it all just worked.

You’d think levels of ridiculousness had peaked; you’d be wrong. Bring back the naked clown. With a popcorn machine strapped to her head, she started hyping up the audience with a dance and hula hoop routine. Then the butter came out, and she slapped it over her body. Turns out if you slap butter on your bum hard enough, it will spray like soap suds. Glad I wasn’t sitting in the butter firing line of the front few rows. Then, in a moment of madness, she released a salt shaker from inside her body to top the buttery popcorn covering the stage. An impressive flourish, anatomically speaking. It had been in there the whole time! I have no artistic explanation for this, and I don’t think one is required.

So yes, Kaye Hole delivered the night we never knew we always wanted. Reuben, like a modern-day 1930s Emcee, kept us on our toes all night, sprinkling political ballads in between the seduction and debauchery. Did I love it? Yes. Will I go back? Yes. Will I take my mum? Probably not.

Seen at McEwan Hall, Edinburgh Fringe, 21st August 2026
